opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so to explain why, it helps to say what the method actually does. We take the model and replace its MLP layers with what we call a cross-layer transcoder. It's trained to reproduce what the MLPs compute, but it does so with sparse, interpretable features. Then for a specific prompt we build an attribution graph showing which features caused which other features, all the way up to the output.

The trick that makes this tractable is that we freeze the attention patterns. For a given prompt, we take where every attention head attended as fixed, and then everything becomes linear and we can cleanly trace influence between features. That works well for one half of attention, what people call the OV circuit. We can see that a feature on token five got moved over to token twelve and contributed to some downstream feature.

What we lose is the *why*. Why did the head look at token five rather than token eight? That's the QK side, the query-key computation that decides where attention goes, and in our graphs it's just treated as a given. A lot of the really interesting computation happens there. Think about a model working out which earlier fact is relevant, or doing in-context retrieval, or tracking which entity a pronoun refers to. Much of that work is choosing what to attend to. So we can end up with a graph that's very clear about the path information took, while the decision that picked the path is hidden.

In practice you see it in our case studies. Sometimes we can tell a really nice story, like the model planning a rhyme or doing multi-hop reasoning. Then other times there's a key step where information just shows up at the right position, and we have to say we can't fully explain why. Researchers then have to go in by hand, look at specific heads, and try to reverse-engineer the attention pattern, and that doesn't scale.

There are also more subtle effects. Since attention is frozen, if you intervene on a feature and that would have changed where the model attends, our linearized picture doesn't capture it. So our predictions about interventions can sometimes be off for exactly that reason.

That's why I'd call it the biggest gap. The MLP side, with transcoders, has gotten to a place where the features are often quite interpretable. Attention is still somewhat of a black box sitting in the middle of the graph. Extending the method so we can explain attention patterns with the same kind of sparse features, and bring QK into the attribution graph, is one of the main things we and others are actively working on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interpretable MLP features and attention as a gap, but does not say that extrapolating current feature coverage shows the approach cannot reach the coverage needed for circuit tracing.

r002.rationale: It says the method treats attention patterns as fixed and leaves unexplained why a head attends to one position rather than another, identifying this as the QK computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way circuit tracing works is we build this replacement model, where we swap out the MLP layers of the model with a cross-layer transcoder. That gives us these interpretable features, and then we can trace how features at one position feed into features at a later layer, and that's how we build the attribution graph. The thing is, when we do that, we freeze the attention patterns. We take the attention weights exactly as they were on the prompt we're studying, and we treat them as fixed. So the graph will tell you that some feature at the token "Texas" contributes to some feature at the final position, and it'll show you an edge there, but what it won't tell you is why the model attended to "Texas" in the first place. That decision, the mechanism that computed the query and key and decided that this token was worth looking at, is just not in the graph. We've essentially hidden it inside a constant.

And that's a big deal, because a lot of the interesting computation in a transformer is in attention. If you think about something like in-context learning, or induction, or the model figuring out which previous token is relevant to the current one, that's all happening in the attention pattern. So in a lot of our case studies, we'll get a really clean story about the features and how they compose, and then we'll hit a spot where the honest answer is "and then an attention head moves this information over, and we don't know how it decided to do that." Sometimes we can go in by hand and look at the head and figure it out, but it's not something the method gives you automatically.

The other piece of this is that the replacement model is only ever an approximation. The features explain a lot of the variance, but there's always this residual error term, and attention is one of the places where that error accumulates, because we're not actually modeling the QK circuit at all. So there's really two problems. One is incompleteness, that we're not explaining a whole class of mechanisms. And the other is that the parts we are explaining are sort of conditioned on the attention being what it was, which means if you perturb the prompt, the graph can change in ways the graph itself can't predict. So I'd say it's the biggest limitation because it's the place where we're most clearly leaving a chunk of the model unexplained, rather than just explaining it imperfectly. And I think dealing with that properly, actually getting interpretable features for queries and keys, is one of the main things we need to make progress on.

r001.rationale: The response says the replacement model is approximate and does not model the QK circuit, but it does not state that extrapolating current feature coverage shows the approach cannot reach the coverage needed for circuit tracing.

r002.rationale: The response says the method freezes attention patterns and leaves out the query/key computations that determine which tokens are attended to.

astra-6.text:
Because attention determines how information moves between tokens, and our circuit-tracing method doesn’t fully explain that routing. We take the attention patterns from the original model’s run and hold them fixed while we build our explanation.

That lets us investigate what information is being passed along those connections and how it contributes to the answer. But it leaves a really important question unanswered: why did the model attend to that token in the first place?

It also limits our interventions. If we change an internal feature, the real model might change where it attends. With attention fixed, we can’t capture that part of the response. So we’re explaining computation along a particular routing pattern, rather than explaining the whole mechanism that produced it. That’s a substantial gap, because choosing where to look is itself a big part of what the model is doing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses attention being fixed and a gap in explaining routing, but does not mention feature coverage or extrapolating coverage to show the approach cannot reach what circuit tracing needs.

r002.rationale: It says attention patterns are held fixed and asks why the model attended to a token in the first place, clearly identifying that the method does not explain the computations determining attention positions.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge with attention is that it moves information between tokens, and our circuit-tracing method doesn’t fully explain how the model decides where to move that information. We essentially take the attention patterns from the original forward pass and hold them fixed while we trace the computation.

That lets us ask, given those attention patterns, what information is being passed around and how is it being used? But it leaves out an important part of the explanation: why did this token attend to that token in the first place?

It also limits our interventions. If we change a feature, we can study its effects with attention held fixed, but the model might actually respond to that change by attending somewhere else. So we get a useful view of the computation, but we’re missing a mechanism that can change the computation itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of tracing attention, but does not say that extrapolated feature coverage falls short of what circuit tracing needs.

r002.rationale: It says the method holds attention patterns fixed and leaves unexplained why one token attends to another, directly identifying the attention-selection computations it does not explain.
